title: [rejected AI] Handle Mapping subclasses in urlencode filter
body:
## What changed

The `urlencode` filter only treated concrete `dict` instances as key/value maps. Any other `Mapping` (such as `collections.UserDict`) fell through to the "iterable of pairs" branch, which iterates the mapping's *keys* and then unpacks each one as a `(key, value)` pair.

For a `UserDict` like `{"Aa": "PersonA@123.com"}`, the key `"Aa"` was unpacked into `("A", "a")`, producing the garbage result `A=a&B=b`. For single-character keys the unpack raises `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)`. Plain `dict` worked, which made the behavior inconsistent with the documented contract ("A dict or iterable of `(key, value)` pairs").

The type check is changed from `isinstance(value, dict)` to `isinstance(value, abc.Mapping)`, so mappings that are not concrete `dict` instances are handled through `value.items()` the same way as `dict`.

## Why

`Mapping` subclasses are valid URL query sources and per the docstring should be treated as key/value pairs. This fixes both the mangled output and the crash, matching the behavior of plain `dict`.

## Tests

Extended the parametrized `test_urlencode` case with:

- `UserDict({"f": 1})` - general non-`dict` mapping with a multi-char key.
- The exact reported scenario: `UserDict({"A": "PersonA@123.com", "B": "PersonB@123.com"})`.

Both fail without the fix (mangled output / `ValueError`) and pass with it.

Validation run locally:

- Full suite: 913 passed (pytest, `filterwarnings=error`).
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`: clean on changed files.
- `mypy` (1.15.0, the pinned CI version): success.

A `CHANGES.rst` entry was added under the unreleased 3.2.0 section.

title: [rejected AI] Ignore the codec warning for unknown string escapes
body:
Fixes #1156.

String literals containing an escape sequence that Python does not know
(e.g. `"\d"` in a regex fragment) are rendered as-is, but the
`unicode-escape` decode in the lexer emits an internal
`DeprecationWarning` for them. The warning points at jinja internals
instead of the user's template, and under strict warning setups
(`-W error`) it becomes a `TemplateSyntaxError` that stops the template
from compiling.

This scopes a `warnings.catch_warnings()` around the decode so the
codec's warning is ignored. Notes:

- rendered output is unchanged — verified across the escape matrix
  (valid escapes, unknown escapes, non-ASCII input, concatenated
  literals, async and sandboxed environments). Changing what an unknown
  escape renders to would be a behaviour break, so this only removes
  the spurious warning;
- malformed sequences (`\xZZ`, `\u12`, `\N{unknown name}`) still raise
  `TemplateSyntaxError` exactly as before;
- checked on Python 3.10, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 — the codec warns with
  `DeprecationWarning` on all of them (verified against CPython 3.14
  source as well).

Adds a regression test that promotes `DeprecationWarning` to an error:
it fails without the fix and passes with it.

title: [rejected AI] tojson: escape U+2028 and U+2029 (JavaScript line/paragraph separators)
body:
## Problem

`htmlsafe_json_dumps` (the `|tojson` filter) escapes `<`, `>`, `&` and `'` so its output is safe to embed in HTML and `<script>` tags. It does **not** escape the Unicode line separator `U+2028` and paragraph separator `U+2029`.

JavaScript treats those two characters as line terminators, exactly like `\n`. When `json.dumps` is told to emit raw Unicode (`ensure_ascii=False`, a very common config), the separators are emitted unescaped, so a crafted string can break out of a `<script>` block:

```python
env.policies['json.dumps_kwargs'] = {'ensure_ascii': False}
template = "{{ x|tojson }}"
# x = '""; alert(1); //\u2028document.location = \"http://evil\"'
```

## Fix

Escape `U+2028` / `U+2029` to `\\u2028` / `\\u2029`, matching what Django's `json_script` filter does. On the default path (`ensure_ascii=True`) `json.dumps` already escapes them as non-ASCII, so the new `.replace()` calls are harmless no-ops there.

Closes #1882

title: [rejected AI] ignore invalid escape sequence warning when unescaping string literals (#1156)
body:
fixes #1156

### Problem

When string literals in templates contain unrecognized escape sequences (such as regex patterns like `"\d"`, `"\w"`, `"\s"`), Python's `decode("unicode-escape")` emits a `DeprecationWarning` (or `SyntaxWarning` in Python 3.12+).

Under strict warning configurations such as `python -Werror` or test suites with warning filters enabled, this warning is converted into an exception during decoding. Jinja's lexer catches this in `except Exception as e:` and raises a `TemplateSyntaxError: invalid escape sequence '\d')`.

### Solution

Wrap the `decode("unicode-escape")` call inside `Lexer.tokeniter` in a warning filter context that ignores `DeprecationWarning` and `SyntaxWarning`. This permits template string literals containing regex patterns or unrecognized escape sequences to be unescaped without raising warnings or failing when `-Werror` is active.

### Verification

- Added unit test `test_unrecognized_escape_sequence` in `tests/test_lexnparse.py` verifying template strings with `\d \w \s` parse and render properly without raising warnings.
- Ran test suite under `-Werror` with pytest: 912/912 tests passed 100% green.
- Ran `ruff check src tests` and `ruff format --check src tests`: all clean.
- Added changelog entry in `CHANGES.rst`.

title: [rejected AI] Do not append fill_with in slice filter when length is divisible
body:
When the length of an iterable is evenly divisible by the slice count (i.e. `length % slices == 0`), each slice already contains the exact same number of elements (`length // slices`). There are no slices with fewer elements, and therefore no missing values to fill.

Previously, `sync_do_slice` checked:
```python
if fill_with is not None and slice_number >= slices_with_extra:
    tmp.append(fill_with)
```

When `slices_with_extra == 0`, `slice_number >= slices_with_extra` evaluated to `slice_number >= 0`, which is `True` for every single slice. As a result, `fill_with` was erroneously appended to every slice. For instance:
```jinja
{{ [1, 2, 3, 4]|slice(4, 'foo')|list }}
```
returned:
```python
[[1, 'foo'], [2, 'foo'], [3, 'foo'], [4, 'foo']]
```
instead of:
```python
[[1], [2], [3], [4]]
```

### Changes
- Updated the `fill_with` condition in `sync_do_slice` to require `slices_with_extra > 0 and slice_number >= slices_with_extra`.
- Added unit test cases for divisible iterable lengths with `fill_with` in both sync and async filter tests (`tests/test_filters.py` and `tests/test_async_filters.py`).
- Added a changelog entry in `CHANGES.rst`.

fixes #2118

Fixes #2118

### Problem
When `slices` evenly divides `len(seq)` (e.g. `[1, 2, 3, 4]|slice(4, 'foo')`), `slices_with_extra = length % slices` is `0`.
Because the check was `slice_number >= slices_with_extra`, every slice satisfied `slice_number >= 0` and had `fill_with` appended, adding an extra unnecessary element to every sub-list even though all slices were already full and of equal length.

### Fix
- Updated the `fill_with` check in `sync_do_slice` in `src/jinja2/filters.py` to require `slices_with_extra > 0` in addition to `slice_number >= slices_with_extra`.
- Added test assertions to `tests/test_filters.py` and `tests/test_async_filters.py`.

title: [rejected AI] LRUCache TypeError on Python 3.14 with unhashable keys
body:
Fixes #2180

Python 3.14 raises a TypeError when an unhashable type (e.g., a dict) appears inside a tuple used as a dict key. The LRUCache in `jinja2/utils.py` uses a plain dict internally, and when a cache key contains an unhashable element, `deque.remove()` internally calls `__hash__` on the key during the linear search, causing a crash.

This fix wraps each key in an `_ImmutableKey` class that uses `object.__hash__` (identity-based hashing), sidestepping the issue entirely. The wrapper is transparent — keys retrieved from the cache are unwrapped before being returned.

**Error before:** `TypeError: cannot use 'tuple' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'dict')`
**After:** Cache works correctly with any key type

title: Reduce lexer backtracking on unclosed strings with many escapes
body:
Fixes the performance issue reported in #2109: the lexer does a lot of redundant work on an unclosed string that contains many escape sequences.

Root cause:
`string_re` matches the body of a quoted string with the unrolled pattern `[^'\\]*(?:\\.[^'\\]*)*` and then requires the closing quote. When the closing quote is missing, the regex engine backtracks through the already matched body, retrying at each position for a quote that is not there. For the input in the issue (a quote, then many `\a` plus a run of `b`, repeated, with no closing quote), that backtracking is expensive.

Fix:
Match the body atomically so the engine does not backtrack into it. Python only gained atomic groups and possessive quantifiers in 3.11, and Jinja supports 3.10, so this uses the lookahead plus backreference form `(?=(...))\N`, which is atomic on 3.10 and later. The lexer only consumes the whole match (`m.group()`), not the inner capture groups, so restructuring the internal groups is safe.

Verification:
- The full test suite passes on Python 3.10, plus a new regression test that lexes the issue's input and confirms it raises `TemplateSyntaxError`.
- The old and new patterns produce identical matches on valid and edge-case strings: empty strings, escaped quotes, escaped backslashes, newlines under `re.S`, adjacent strings, a trailing backslash, and unterminated strings (both reject).
- On the issue's input the new pattern is about 5 times faster. On ordinary valid strings the extra lookahead pass is negligible (about a microsecond per match over 300k matches).

Per the maintainers' note in the issue, this is a performance fix, not a security report, so no CVE is requested.

## Bug

When the slice count divides the iterable length evenly, the `slice` filter still pads every chunk with `fill_with`:

Expected: `[[1], [2], [3], [4]]`

## Cause

In `sync_do_slice`, the padding condition is `slice_number >= slices_with_extra`. When `length % slices == 0`, `slices_with_extra` is 0, so the condition is true for every chunk and each one gets `fill_with` appended — even though no chunk is short.

## Fix

Only pad when there are short chunks to pad, i.e. when `slices_with_extra` is non-zero. The non-divisor behavior (padding the chunks after the extras, e.g. `range(10)|slice(3, 'X')` → `[[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6, 'X'], [7, 8, 9, 'X']]`) is unchanged.

## Tests

Added a regression test for the divisor case. Full suite:

```
912 passed in 2.49s
```

title: Do not report names assigned by every if branch as undeclared
body:
`meta.find_undeclared_variables` reports a name that is `{% set %}` in every branch of an `{% if %}` chain ending in `{% else %}`, even though such a name is always defined afterwards and is never read from the context:

```python
env.parse("{% if a %}{% set x = 1 %}{% else %}{% set x = 2 %}{% endif %}{{ x }}")
# reports {"a", "x"}; "x" cannot come from the context
```

### Why it regressed

`Symbols.branch_update` used to skip the context load for a name stored by every branch. #1665 removed that optimisation to fix #1253, because it also skipped the load when a branch *read* the name before assigning it.

### This change

Restores the optimisation behind two guards:

1. Every branch must introduce the name as a fresh local, that is, its load is `undefined` rather than `resolve`/`alias`. This is the case #1253 needed.
2. The name must not be read inside a scope `FrameSymbolVisitor` does not enter. Those reads are invisible to the frame's symbols but still read the frame's variables, so `FrameSymbolVisitor` now records them and `visit_If` consults them. Every field the compiler visits with a child frame is tracked: `For.body/else_/test`, `Macro.body/defaults`, `CallBlock.body/defaults`, `FilterBlock.body/filter`, `With.body`, `AssignBlock.body/filter`, `Scope.body`, `Block.body`, `OverlayScope.context/body`.

`visit_If` also tracks each `{% elif %}` body as its own branch, so plain `{% if %}`/`{% else %}` is recognised too. That case was reported in #2069 as failing on 3.1.4 as well.

The scan of nested scopes is lazy, so a frame with no exhaustive `{% if %}` chain does no extra work.

### Verification

- The three snippets in #2069 (with `elif`, without `elif`, and the no-`else` control case) all behave as the reporter expected.
- Differential run over ~1260 generated templates x 8 contexts covering `for`, `for recursive`, `macro`, `call`, `filter`, `with`, `set`/`endset`, `block`, `extends`, `include`, `import`, namespaces, tuple targets and nested chains: no rendered output changes, only the intended reduction in `find_undeclared_variables` results.
- Compile time measured at roughly +2% on a 200-unit page template.

### Tests

- `tests/test_api.py` — parametrized `find_undeclared_variables` cases, including the negative ones: no `else`, a branch that does not assign, read-before-assign, read in an `elif` test, read in a nested scope.
- `tests/test_regression.py` — rendering tests beside the existing #1253 test, covering a read in each child-frame field.
- `tests/test_idtracking.py` — symbol-level assertions for an exhaustive chain and for `OverlayScope.context`.

Full suite: 936 passed. `ruff` clean; `mypy` reports the same pre-existing errors as `main`.

fixes #2069

title: AI junk
body:
fixes #2176

`do_indent` ends with an unconditional prepend:

```python
if first:
    rv = indention + rv
```

So `first=True` indents the first line even when it is empty, right after `blank=False` finished skipping every other empty line. The result is trailing whitespace on a line with nothing on it.

```pycon
>>> Environment().from_string("{% filter indent(4, first=True) %}{% endfilter %}").render()
'    '
```

In the reporter's template that shows up as an empty `{% block %}` inside `{% filter indent(4, first=True) %}` leaving four spaces that shift the following line, so the base template only renders correctly when a child happens to override the block.

## Why `blank` wins

The two arguments look like they conflict, but they answer different questions:

- `first` — is the first line special? (`True`: no, treat it like the rest.)
- `blank` — are empty lines indented? (`False`: no.)

An empty first line is both, so once `first=True` says "not special", it falls under the ordinary empty-line rule and `blank` decides. Reading it the other way makes `first=True` mean "treat the first line like the others, except give it the indentation the others would not get".

```python
if first and (blank or rv.partition(newline)[0]):
    rv = indention + rv
```

## Heads-up: this changes an assertion

`_test_indent_multiline_template` feeds text beginning with a newline and asserts:

```python
t = env.from_string("{{ foo|indent(2, true, false) }}")
assert t.render(foo=text) == '  \n  foo bar\n  "baz"\n'
```

That leading `'  '` is the bug, so the assertion is updated rather than preserved. Flagging it explicitly because it means someone could be relying on the old output: anyone passing `first=True, blank=False` with a leading newline loses two spaces on line one. Adding a separate opt-in flag seemed worse than fixing `blank` to mean what it says, but that is a maintainer call and I am happy to redo it that way.

`blank=True` is untouched: an empty first line is still indented there, which is what opting into blank-line indentation should do.

## Tests

New `test_indent_blank_first_line_not_indented_without_blank` covers the four cases that pin the rule:

| Input | Args | Expected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `""` (empty filter body) | `first=True` | `""` |
| `"\nsecond"` | `first=True` | `"\n  second"` |
| `"\nsecond"` | `first=True, blank=True` | `"  \n  second"` |
| `"first\nsecond"` | `first=True` | `"  first\n  second"` |

The third and fourth are there so the fix cannot be over-applied: it would be easy to drop the leading indent for every `first=True` case, or to break `blank=True`, and both would pass with only the first two.

```
$ pytest -q
912 passed in 0.76s

$ ruff check src tests    All checks passed!
$ ruff format --check     49 files already formatted
```

Docstring for `blank` now states the interaction, and there is a `CHANGES.rst` entry under 3.2.0 noting the behaviour change.

title: AI junk
body:
## Problem

`copy.copy(Template(...))` and `copy.deepcopy(Template(...))` both raise:

```
TypeError: __new__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'source'
```

## Root cause

`Template.__new__(cls, source, ...)` requires a `source` argument. The default copy/deepcopy path calls `cls.__new__(cls)` with no arguments, which fails.

## Fix

Add `__copy__` and `__deepcopy__` to `Template` that build the clone via `object.__new__(cls)` and share the immutable render-time state (compiled code, environment, globals, blocks, root render function, etc.).

A shallow copy is the correct behavior for deepcopy as well: templates hold compiled code, shared globals, and render functions that must not be independently deep-copied — otherwise the copy would diverge from the original's compiled form.

## Testing

Added two regression tests to `tests/test_pickle.py`:

- `test_template_copy` — verifies `copy.copy` produces a working, independent template
- `test_template_deepcopy` — verifies `copy.deepcopy` produces a working, independent template

All three tests in the file pass:

```
tests/test_pickle.py::test_environment PASSED
tests/test_pickle.py::test_template_copy PASSED
tests/test_pickle.py::test_template_deepcopy PASSED
```

Fixes #758

## Summary

This simplifies `_PassArg.from_obj` to read `jinja_pass_arg` with one `getattr(..., None)` call instead of checking with `hasattr` and then reading the attribute again.

body:
## Summary
Fixes #2118.

`slice(n, fill_with)` incorrectly appended a filler to **every** column when the sequence length was evenly divisible by `n`:

```jinja
{{ [1, 2, 3, 4]|slice(4, 'foo')|list }}
```

- **Before:** `[[1, 'foo'], [2, 'foo'], [3, 'foo'], [4, 'foo']]`
- **After:** `[[1], [2], [3], [4]]`

### Root cause
Padding used `slice_number >= slices_with_extra`. When the remainder is `0`, that is true for **all** slices, so every full column got one extra filler.

### Fix
Pad only when `len(tmp) < target`, where `target` is the tallest column height. Uneven cases still pad shorter columns as before.

### Tests
- Regression for even divisor + `fill_with`
- Existing slice cases still pass

body: The code generator formats the template name into the "no else section" message for a failing inline if-expression by writing self.position(node) straight into a double-quoted string literal in the generated module, so a name that contains a double quote breaks out of that literal. When such a template renders an inline if without an else branch and the condition is false, compiling the generated code raises a SyntaxError, or runs code injected through the name (a name of the form `a", <python>, "b` reaches the generated module verbatim). This is the same shape as the FromImport case that was already escaped for GHSA-gmj6-6f8f-6699; here I build the message and write it through repr so quotes and other characters are escaped consistently. Added a regression test in tests/test_compile.py using a quoted template name, which fails with a SyntaxError before the change.

body:
Fixes #2176.

## Problem

When `s` is empty, `indent(first=True)` unconditionally indents it even
though `blank` defaults to `False`, producing whitespace-only output for
content that has nothing to indent:

```python
Environment().from_string("{% filter indent(4, first=True) %}{% endfilter %}").render()
# expected: ""
# actual:   "    "
```

## Fix

Track whether the original input was non-empty before the `s += newline`
quirk, and only apply the first-line indent when `blank=True` or the input
actually had content:

```python
if first and (blank or had_content):
    rv = indention + rv
```

This is deliberately narrower than treating "first line is blank" as the
trigger. A previous attempt at this issue (#2181) took that broader
approach, but it would have changed the existing documented behavior for
multi-line input whose first line happens to be blank while later lines
have content — `test_indent` / `_test_indent_multiline_template` already
assert that `first=True` indents a blank first line in that case, and I
wanted to preserve that. This fix only special-cases the case where there
is no real content at all.

## Testing

- Added `test_indent_first_on_empty_string` covering both `blank=False`
  (default) and `blank=True`.
- Full test suite: `912 passed`.
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check`: clean.
